questions.prompt: Which of these is a force?
options: A push or a pull acting on an object
questions.explanation: Force is defined as a push or a pull — an interaction that can change an object's motion.
questions.misconception: Some imagine force as a substance stored inside objects (like warmth). Force is an interaction, not a property of stuff.

questions.prompt: What unit is used to measure force?
questions.explanation: Force is measured in newtons (N), named for Sir Isaac Newton.
questions.misconception: kg is a mass unit and kg·m/s² the hidden form of the newton; mixing the two is the classic slip.

questions.prompt: Why are forces usually drawn as arrows?
options: Because a force has both a size and a direction
Because arrows are the only shape allowed
Because newtons add up to meters
questions.explanation: An arrow shows the magnitude (length) and the direction (heading) of a force in one picture.
questions.misconception: Treating a force as a plain number ignores its direction — the arrow is exactly the vector lesson.

questions.prompt: Two equal forces push a box in opposite directions. What is the net force?
options: Twice the size of one force
Half the size of one force
questions.explanation: Equal forces in opposite directions cancel to zero net force, so there is nothing left over to change the motion.
questions.misconception: It's tempting to add 10 + 10 = 20, but direction must be considered: opposite arrows subtract.

questions.prompt: A 50 N push east faces a 20 N pull the opposite way. What is the net force?
questions.explanation: The two arrows partly cancel: 50 − 20 = 30 N pointing the stronger way, east.
questions.misconception: Adding instead of subtracting gets 70 N; remembering opposite arrows subtract is the whole point of the net.
